headlines.title: Terra restaurant inside San Jose's Eataly closes due to vermin contamination, officials say
headlines.description: The Terra restaurant on the third floor of Eataly closed due to vermin contamination, according to the County of Santa Clara Environmental Health on Friday. Authorities said an inspection was conducted in the entire Eataly food facility after the department received a public complaint denouncing the presence of rodents. They said that, although the investigation did not find rodents, it confirmed the presence of vermin on the third floor. According to the Department of Environmental Health Official Inspection Report, the inspector “found a live cockroach crawling on the wall above the hand wash sink in the kitchen.” The report also stated they found “dead cockroaches in the following areas: on the wall above the hand wash sink in the food preparation area.” The health permit for Terra Restaurant and Bar was then suspended, according to health authorities. They said the restaurant manager confirmed during an interview with Environmental Health inspectors that pest control services were completed Thursday night, the facility was thoroughly cleaned and sanitized and food that was potentially contaminated was thrown away. Officials said the restaurant will reopen as soon as it resolves all open items from the inspection report and requests a reinspection to confirm the problem was resolved. NBC Bay Area reached out to Eataly for comment but hasn’t heard back.

headlines.title: Proposed innovation center in downtown Oakland triggers questions, concerns
headlines.description: A proposed project in the heart of downtown Oakland, referred to by some as a data center, is raising concerns about its environmental impact and actual economic benefits, but the developer insists it is not a data center. Behring Companies said it’s planning to convert some 20,000 square feet of a building on 20th Street into what it calls an innovation campus. “Data center is typically a bunch of racks and computers for outside parties,” Colin Behring said. “It’s dark. There’s no people in it. That’s not what we can do here.” Behring said the facility could provide computing power for AI, robotics and other tech startups as part of a larger innovation campus surrounding the 19th Street BART station. The building has a history of housing computers. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory once operated a federal supercomputing facility at the site, which Behring said makes it easier to convert the building to house shelves of memory-rich computers now. Many call that a data center, and they have questions about the environmental footprint along with water and power usage. Behring said that wouldn’t be a problem with their center. “California produces so much power that we actually throw away like 3.5 million megawatts of solar and other clean energy every single year because we can’t even store it,” Behring said. District 3 Councilmember Carroll Fife organized a community meeting Friday to let people question the developer directly. Fife said she wants to make sure there are benefits to the average Oakland resident. “We know of all of the concerns that have happened across the country with these large-scale mega facilities coming into low-income communities, people of color communities that don’t have the resources to push back,” she said. Fife said the Oakland Planning and Building Department received Behring’s proposal a week ago for an AI campus. “I want it to be absolutely, critically clear that this is not the large-scale mega facility that people have expressed,” Fife said.

headlines.title: Bay Area woman aims to be the first to swim the whole California coast
headlines.description: Catherine Breed, 33, is nearly midway through her journey to swim around 900 miles, from the California-Oregon border to Mexico. The long-distance swimmer is believed to be the first to attempt swimming the entirety of the California coast, an attempt she began on July 1 and is expected to continue through November. Breed is swimming in the open ocean, accompanied by a boat and a team helping her along the way. Breed grew up in Pleasanton, graduating from Amador Valley High School. She went on to swim for U.C. Berkeley and the U.S. National team. After college, she developed a love for open water swimming through the Dolphin Club in San Francisco. Breed has now achieved several ultra-long-distance swims, including swimming the length of Lake Tahoe and swimming from San Francisco to Half Moon Bay. At each stop along Breed’s swim, she is holding community events to highlight community organizations and coastal issues. “How do we stop and make it a little poetic, and make it a love letter to the coast, and enjoy this place?” Breed explained to a crowd in San Francisco. Friday evening, she stopped in San Francisco near Crissy Field for a meet-and-greet event to promote local ocean conservation efforts, hosted by the Greater Farallones & Cordell Bank National Marine Sanctuaries and partnered with the Bay Area-based Marine Mammal Center. “It’s just so wonderful to see Cat doing something that celebrates our ocean and bringing the community together, so that we can learn how to all care for [the ocean] to the best of our ability,” said Katie D’Innocenzo with the Marine Mammal Center. D’Innocenzo noted that during Breed’s swim, she is encountering the same coastal issues the Marine Mammal Center is tracking, such as warming El Niño ocean waters. Many of Breed’s friends and family from the Bay Area showed up, as did a number of people who’ve been following her journey on social media. “Being home has been really special, because I do get to be home, I get to see my family, I get to see my friends,” Breed told NBC Bay Area News in an interview on Friday. “It’s also challenging because it’s the middle of the swim, and because I still have a long ways to go,” she continued. But Breed noted getting to be around her Bay Area loved ones was “just a perfect morale boost after getting through one of the hardest stretches of Swim California.” Swim California is what Breed is calling her journey. As of Friday, Breed swam a total of 450 miles of the state’s coast, with 550 more miles remaining. She is hoping her swim inspires others — especially women — to explore and care for the ocean. “What I want people to know is how amazing the ocean is, and how much I am learning with every stroke that I take,” Breed said. She encouraged Bay Area residents to “come to a community event and learn about what’s going on in the ocean conservation space in your backyard.” Breed will continue her swim Saturday morning in San Francisco, continuing her swim south from Ocean Beach.

headlines.title: Crews work to restore Big Basin trails following massive fire
headlines.description: In the last six years since the CZU Lightning Complex fire humbled the giant redwoods of Big Basin Redwoods State Park in the Santa Cruz Mountains, the park has slowly crawled back to life. Astride the blackened, hollowed carcasses of fallen trees, some trails have reopened, and there are plans to replace some of the infrastructure erected over the last century which the fire reduced to cinders. But a new effort is underway to restore some of the once-popular trails deeper in the forest which remain closed to the public. Every day, a crew of state park employees and the California Conservation Corps trek a mile and a half down meandering trails, past downed trees, often hauling lumber, tools, and fiberglass planks to rebuild the paths and the 22 pedestrian bridges that burned. The group has cleared massive logs and hazardous trees and erected retaining walls to shore up trails that were washed away. “We’re blazing about four to five miles of trail to create a loop from Skyline-to-the-Sea, Timms Creek and Sunset Trail,” said Eamon Reynolds of California State Parks. Timms Creek trail bears all the telltale signs of the recent disaster: fallen logs, landslides and gaps where bridges stood. The crews have had to cut away the overgrown vegetation and recut the paths through the thick forest. They’re rebuilding bridges using fiberglass in place of the original wood. “They’re all made of fiberglass,” said Reynolds. “And they are for many reasons fire resistant as well as they don’t rot.” A crew from California Conservation Corps works to restore Timms Creek trail in Big Basin Redwoods State Park, which burned in the 2020 CZU Lightning Complex Fire. Before the fire, the 4.5-mile Timms Creek loop was a popular trail, connecting to other trails in the system and ultimately the Pacific Ocean below. Reynolds said when the project wrap ups, he expects it will become popular again. “One of my dreams is just getting this section of trail open again,” Reynolds said. “It will be really good to see all those people come down here like they once did before the fire.” The work is an opportunity for the youth-driven California Conservation Corps to cut their teeth as well. The workforce training program gives young people a chance to gain trade experience for future careers. CCC member Coltrane Mueller has spent months alongside his fellow crew members sawing fallen trees and shaping trails. “Legacy feels like a strong word,” Mueller said. “But to leave a legacy, and if I ever have kids, I could bring them here and be like, ‘I built that.’” Sempervirens Fund, the group formed 126 years ago to protect the redwoods of Big Basin — California’s first state park — is fundraising $450,000 to help pay for the project. The vision is to make the park more resistant to future wildfires, which are expected to increase in frequency with the changing climate. A crew from California Conservation Corps works to restore Timms Creek trail in Big Basin Redwoods State Park, which burned in the 2020 CZU Lightning Complex Fire. “I think one of the important things about this project is we are building back these trails better than they were and in a way that’s going to be more resilient than the old way,” Sempervirens Executive Director Sara Barth said. The trail is expected to reopen in spring 2027, allowing visitors a backcountry trek that feels like a true escape. Barth said since its inception, Big Basin has been a catalyst for preservation – and in this case restoration. “Big Basin taught Californians what a state park could be,” Barth said. “I think today Big Basin is teaching us how we have a park exist in a land that burns regularly.” Bay Area Feb 19 Santa Cruz County Jan 13, 2022 Introducing Gateway to Big Basin: New Park Coming to Santa Cruz Mountains

headlines.title: ‘I have a lot to live for': Greg Papa opens up about cancer fight, family and job
headlines.description: In his own words. Greg Papa sat down with NBC Bay Area for his first television interview since recent health complications from his cancer diagnosis. NBC Bay Area’s Raj Mathai met with the legendary broadcaster at his home in Marin County for a wide-ranging interview that focused on facing death, family, being laid off by KNBR and more. “I do not want to die,” Papa said. “I’m going to fight as hard as I can, fight to stay alive. I have a lot to live for.” For decades, Papa’s voice has brought to life some of the most colorful sports moments. He’s given the Bay Area memories that span generations from his time covering the A’s and Raiders to the Warriors, Giants and 49ers. These days, his voice is strong and still resonates, but the game has changed. Doctors diagnosed him with leukemia last summer. He got sick while vacationing in France. “There were many nights there that I felt, you know, I may die,” Papa said. “Cancer is unfair. Cancer is sudden. Cancer is cruel.” His lifeline turned out to be his bloodline. His younger sister, Judy, was a perfect match. In March, she donated her stem cells for a bone marrow transplant. A month later, things took a turn for the worse. Complications from the transplant caused pneumonia, and his lungs collapsed. He nearly died and spent 78 days in the ICU. “I was put on a ventilator,” Papa said. “I was intubated. I was in an induced coma for about five days. It went from a life-threatening situation for certain to a life-altering one…I’ve made a lot of progress since I’ve been home. I made a lot progress since late July.” He continues his fight and wants to get back to what he loves in the radio booth. “I’m cleared, by the way, to go back on the radio show that I had that I no longer have,” he said. In early August, Papa was laid off by KNBR. In his first public comments since the layoff, he said, “I was fully preparing to return to work. There was never discussion that that would not be the case. And then one day you get a phone call and I thought it was a return-to-work plan…I was cleared, my hematologist cleared me [for the radio show] and they went the other way and they chose to terminate my contract.” Cumulus Media, which owns KNBR, issued a statement on Aug. 7 acknowledging Papa’s departure, writing, “our respect and gratitude for everything Greg has given to KNBR, its listeners, and its team runs deep. We are continuing to explore ways we can bring his voice back to the station, and we wish Greg strength, healing, and a full recovery.” Papa still has his job as the San Francisco 49ers radio announcer. He said he’d like to come back sometime this season to call games, but he didn’t know if that was possible. The David Benzer Strike Out Fear Foundation has set up a GoFund Me campaign to help with the financial burden of Papa’s long recovery.
headlines.source: Raj Mathai, Christine Ni and Alex Bozovic

headlines.title: Bay Area residents traveling to Hawaii prepare for historic Tropical Storm Lala
headlines.description: One of Bay Area residents’ most popular destination spots is prepping for a very unwanted visitor; Tropical Storm Lala is bearing down on the Hawaiian Islands. As the weather changes, preparations have been getting more intense. While many local travelers said they’re not changing their plans, they are keeping an eye on the skies. Tropical Storm Lala is forecasted to turn into a Category 1 hurricane heading toward the Big Island. It could be the first hurricane on record to ever make landfall on the Big Island and the first hurricane to hit the state of Hawaii in more than 30 years. Tropical Storm Lala is expected to whip up hazardous ocean conditions and heavy rain is expected in Maui. The Honolulu Zoo is taking steps to protect its animals as the islands, especially the Big Island, are preparing for heavy rain. An emergency has now been declared. “Usually, the tropical systems, as they approach the Hawaiian Islands, start to weaken, but this time we seeing it possibly strengthen as we go through the weekend,” NBC Bay Area Meteorologist Kari Hall said. Meanwhile, Bay Area travelers on their way to Hawaii say they’re watching the weather, but aren’t ready to cancel their Hawaiian dreams. “You know, I need to see my dad so I’m gonna go, and I trust Hawaiian Airlines, right, they are the best airline,” traveler Plyfaa Sewanamalyk-Murphy said. Some said they’ve been through island storms before. “Beautiful, it’s raining, everything’s calm, it’s almost like a facade is lifted and you’re really getting the true experience of nature,” traveler Vartan Kendirdjian said. Others returned home through SFO on Friday before the storm. “It was a little busy, but it was totally fine. Clear skies but a lot of people were trying to get on this flight, there were people on standby, crossing their fingers, hoping to get on,” Oakland resident Dylan said. Dylan was at a work trip on the Big Island when he heard about the tropical storm. Other travelers in Hawaii were scrambling to do the same. For those whose flight is cancelled because of the weather, travel experts said they have the right to a refund or rebooking, both for flights and hotels. Airbnb also has a major disruption policy.

headlines.title: 2028 MLB All-Star Game coming to San Francisco's Oracle Park
headlines.description: The 2028 MLB All-Star Game will be played in San Francisco’s Oracle Park, adding another major sporting event to the Bay Area’s calendar. The San Francisco Giants and Mayor Daniel Lurie’s office confirmed the game is scheduled for July 12. “With its passionate fanbase, world-class ballpark, and rich baseball history, San Francisco will be an outstanding host for All-Star Week, which culminates in one of Major League Baseball’s best traditions, the Midsummer Classic,” MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred said in a statement. “We look forward to bringing the excitement of All-Star Week and the celebration of baseball to the Bay Area.” The last time the All-Star Game was played at the Giants’ ballpark was in 2007. The announcement comes amid a busy stretch for Bay Area sports, with the region also hosting Super Bowl LX, the 2025 NBA All-Star Game and the FIFA World Cup 2026. Lurie celebrated the announcement on social media, pointing to the city’s focus on public safety and clean streets. “We’ve made public safety our top priority since day one, and we’re delivering safe and clean streets for residents and visitors,” Lurie said. “Now, people want to be here again.” MLB Aug 14 Jackson Flora Aug 12 Mike Krukow Aug 11 The Giants will host the Midsummer Classic for a fourth time overall after Candlestick Park held the first All-Star Game of the 1961 season and also baseball’s summer showcase in 1984. Oracle Park is set to become the eighth active ballpark to hold the All-Star Game multiple times, joining Fenway Park in 1946, 1961 and 1999, Wrigley Field (1947, 1962, 1990), Angel Stadium (1967, 1989, 2010), Dodger Stadium (1980, 2022), Progressive Field (1997, 2019), Coors Field (1998, 2021) and T-Mobile Park (2001, 2023). Giants President and CEO Larry Baer said the club is “incredibly honored” and expressed his gratitude. “This is a tremendous opportunity to showcase our organization, our city, and the incredible passion of our fans on baseball’s biggest summer stage,” he said in a statement. “Hosting the All-Star Game is more than celebrating the game’s brightest stars, it’s a chance to highlight the people, neighborhoods, and culture that make our community so special. Few cities offer the unique combination of sports, culture, innovation, entertainment, and natural beauty that defines San Francisco. We look forward to welcoming players, families, fans, and visitors from around the world for a week that will create lasting memories and have a meaningful impact throughout our region.”
headlines.source: NBC Bay Area staff and The Associated Press

headlines.title: 47-year-old man joins San Jose City College football team
headlines.description: A South Bay pastor made his college football comeback at the age of 47. Justin Buzzard, 47, joined the San Jose City College football team, the Jaguars. Buzzard was inspired to try after seeing a social media video of a man in his 60s playing football in the East Coast. He reached out to a coach at SJCC, and after giving it some thought, he decided to go for it and he made it. Buzzard joined NBC Bay Area’s Raj Mathai to talk more about his new path. Watch the full interview in the video above.

headlines.title: All 16 Livermore abandoned puppies have been adopted, shelter says
headlines.description: The East Bay SPCA nonprofit shelter shared that all 16 abandoned puppies found in a Livermore Walmart parking lot back in July have been adopted. On July 8, local advocates who help with rescuing lost and missing animals were alerted to a large group of puppies in a brushy area outside the Livermore Walmart parking lot. Unfortunately, one of the puppies there had been hit and killed by a car. Good samaritans corralled the sixteen surviving puppies into their cars and took them to East Bay SPCA, which has a contract with the city of Livermore to take in the city’s lost, injured, or stray animals. The puppies were then given the veterinary care they needed and put up for adoption. While all the puppies did look similar, shelter staff estimate that there could be more than one litter of puppies in this group. “Young animals do tend to get adopted quickly,” said Jes Cytron, the Vice President of Operations for East Bay SPCA. She continued, “What we didn’t really expect was that with the influx of attention the puppies brought to us, we also had community members come in search of adult dogs, and some of our long-term adult dogs also found homes.”

headlines.title: Family and friends remember teen killed in mass shooting near Morgan Hill
headlines.description: A memorial service was held on Friday for the young man shot and killed during a party near Morgan Hill in July. Desiderio Romero V, 18, was remembered by family and friends during a service held at the Santa Teresa Catholic Church in San Jose. “At the end, you pray to God and give you strength and we’re getting through it pretty good, I mean, as best as we can,” Desiderio Romero III, Desiderio Romero the Fifth’s grandfather said. The young man was killed, and six others injured, during a mass shooting on July 25 at an unsanctioned pop-up birthday party in an open field near Morgan Hill. Police say the gathering included about 300 people. Romero’s family says his decision to go to the party was apparently spur of the moment. “It was something ‘online’ that they sent out to a bunch of people and it was like two hours before the thing happened,” Desiderio Romero III said. Romero V’s grandfather says their last words to each other were “I love you,” and that gives him comfort. “Because if those are your last words that you hear or you gave to them, it’s like I can live with that. I mean it hurts, but the words for him to say ‘I love you poppy’, or grandpa, I mean those… I’ll never forget,” he said. That love and the regret was expressed by many. “And I feel it is such a ‘waste’ of life for a child to be taken away this quickly and in that manner,” Andre Hunt, a family friend, said. The grandfather says the sheriff’s updates on the investigation have him feeling optimistic about an arrest, but he did not want to say more to avoid complicating the case. “I hope we find him, I hope that he has to pay for this. It’s not a vengeance thing, it’s like, to ‘kill’ somebody,” Romero III said. The sheriff’s office did not provide any specific details updating the case, saying only that deputies are pursuing leads and asking anyone who might have any information, especially video from the party, to contact investigators.

headlines.title: DA seeks adult charges for teen accused in Fairfield graduation shooting
headlines.description: A minor charged with killing a young man after his high school graduation ceremony in Fairfield may be tried as an adult following a petition from the Solano County District Attorney’s Office. On Tuesday, 17-year-old Khare Clark appeared in juvenile court to plead not guilty to charges of murder and several counts of attempted murder in the shooting death of 18-year-old Jamario Baker. On June 3, Clark allegedly opened fire in the parking lot of Sem Yeto High School following the school’s graduation ceremony. An 11-year-old and two adults were also injured in the shooting. Around 1,000 people attended the ceremony, according to the district attorney’s office. Clark was arrested in Texas in July following a monthlong investigation and was extradited to California for trial. A hearing date to transfer Clark to adult court will be set at a proceeding scheduled in September. According to the district attorney’s office, Clark will be transferred to adult court “if and only if” it is decided he will not be rehabilitated if placed under the authority of juvenile court.

headlines.title: New housing development opens in East San Jose
headlines.description: A new housing development aimed at helping working families afford homes in the Bay Area has opened in East San Jose. City and community leaders celebrated the opening of The Kirk, an 18-home, single-family housing development. The community includes two below-market-rate homes for qualified buyers, as well as tax incentives for first-time homebuyers. San Jose Mayor Matt Mahan said the development is part of a broader effort to address the city’s affordable housing crisis. The homes are 100% electric and solar-ready.
